corrected_statement: Below an effective size of 300 (n_plan: units for a number, events or the rarest class's count for a class outcome, in one outer training fold), the plan draws no Sobol candidates and boosted trees and XGBoost fit once at the library defaults (tuning.SMALL_N, searched_size). The documented reason (RECIPES §4.6) is only that settings chosen on few units vary from sample to sample and can miscalibrate (Riley et al. 2021, for penalized regression); the app never established that the defaults predict as well as nested tuning, and its 2026-10-11 ruling (RECIPES §4.6, WAVE_C6A §7 ruling 16) replaces the library defaults below 300 with a small-sample standard that the code does not yet implement.
source_note: Verified Riley et al. 2021, J Clin Epidemiol 132:88-96 (PMID 33307188) via Europe PMC: tuning parameters 'estimated with large uncertainty ... of most concern when development data sets have a small effective sample size'; 'can lead to considerable miscalibration'. The study covers uniform shrinkage, ridge, lasso and elastic net only, not boosted trees or XGBoost, and recommends larger samples, not library defaults. Van Calster 2020 and Martin 2021 are also regression shrinkage papers (not fetched). RECIPES §4.6 states '300 is a convention'. The repo's own held-out study (docs/turbotab-next/notes/SMALL_SAMPLE_STANDARD.md §2, 14 cells) finds the library defaults the worst arm in every cell: regret 0.10-0.23 nats for boosted trees and 0.15-0.39 for XGBoost, calibration slopes about 0.3. It contradicts the 'at least as well and better calibrated' part. RECIPES §4.6 now records this as Ruled (2026-10-11).
note: That test pins the plan to a direct HistGradientBoosting() fit bit for bit, so it checks the behavior, not the claim. test_rt5a_t1_nested_tuning.py only reports nested tuning against the standard settings and does not assert it. The repo's own evidence refutes the claim, and the ruled fix is not built: boosted_trees.py:71 and xgboost_family.py:502 still declare the library defaults, and the methods text (boosted_trees.py:289) still says they are 'used alone below an effective size of 300'. The 'too few to rank settings' tuning line in RECIPES §4.6 was not found in the code.

corrected_statement: Under inference with repeated units at or above the unit floor (8, seal.min_groups via utils/test_lockbox.py:70), GEE with an exchangeable working correlation reports CR2 (BRL) intervals on Bell-McCaffrey degrees of freedom; for a numeric outcome this keeps type I error at or below about 8% with 12 units. Below the floor, floor_refusal refuses the intervals. The exits are combining each unit's rows or, for a numeric outcome only, the random-intercept mixed model; for a yes/no outcome the second exit is a random-intercept logistic model, which is not yet in TurboTab.
source_note: Verified McCaffrey & Bell 2006, Stat Med 25:4081-4098 (PMID 16456895), abstract via NCBI efetch. BRL with Satterthwaite df gives 'near-nominal type I error rates when the ICC is small'; it 'works less well when the ICC is large' but still beats the sandwich. The abstract names no specific cluster count such as 12. Liang & Zeger 1986 is the GEE method itself (not fetched). The floor of 8 is a repo constant (_MIN_GROUPS_FOR_GROUPED_LOCKBOX) with no methods source cited.
note: The test is a known-truth null simulation: 12 units of 6-10 rows, a unit-level exposure with no effect, ICC about 0.59, 300 replicates. It asserts rejection <= 8% (MC SE 0.013) and that the uncorrected sandwich rejects more. It certifies the numeric-outcome case only: there is no binary GEE type I error test, and the bound is one-sided, so an over-conservative interval would pass. Note that the test is stronger than the source, which warns of degraded BRL performance at large ICC. I could not run the test: pytest is not installed in .venv. The 'refused below the floor' part is a design rule (floor_refusal); test_the_shelf_orders_the_exits_by_soundness_for_the_purpose checks the shelf's ranking at 6 units.

corrected_statement: For a yes/no outcome, no resampling or class weighting is applied by default, because resampling overestimates the rarer class's probability without raising the AUC (van den Goorbergh et al. 2022, logistic regression); a decision moves the threshold instead. Explore offers an opt-in correction (weights, undersample or oversample) that is fitted in-fold and followed by logistic recalibration. However, the 'No resampling ... or class weighting was applied' sentence is emitted for every binary fit, including fits where that lever is on.
source_note: Verified van den Goorbergh, van Smeden, Timmerman & Van Calster, JAMIA 2022;29(9):1525-1534 (PMID 35686364) via Europe PMC. Random undersampling, random oversampling and SMOTE 'yielded poorly calibrated models: the probability to belong to the minority class was strongly overestimated' and 'did not result in higher areas under the ROC curve'; 'similar results were obtained by shifting the probability threshold instead'. The regime is standard and ridge logistic regression only. Class weighting was not studied, nor were tree ensembles or boosting, which the sentence also covers.
note: The certification is partial. A known-truth simulation (logistic truth, 8% events, 40,000 fresh rows) asserts that weights, undersampling and oversampling, unrecalibrated, raise the mean predicted risk above 2.5 times the event rate. That covers the overestimation half, for logistic regression only. The 'without raising the AUC' half is only sourced, and SMOTE is not implemented. test_wp9_validation_performance.py::test_e15 pins wording only. It goes to review for a code/text mismatch: modeling.py:2384 calls imbalance_sentence unconditionally, while pipeline.py:537 applies ImbalanceCorrected when levers.imbalance != 'none'. A run with the lever on would therefore state that nothing was resampled or weighted.

corrected_statement: Before the lock, the app ranks the energy-screen noticing with an outcome-blind design-space proxy: the share of rows the screen removes times the leavers' largest SMD on the adjustment set (Austin 2009 SMD; per level for categories). It bands that proxy against conventional thresholds (SURFACING_POLICY §2.4 started at 0.05 and 0.2). On 9 cases from one NHANES fixture, the band-1 threshold was lowered to 0.0037 so that no case falls below noise falsely, which in practice floors nearly every screen at 'could bias'. The band is a pre-lock recommendation only. After the lock, the every-row refit verifies it, and the exhibit is relabeled openly when the realized movement is larger. The app does not claim the proxy predicts the movement in half-widths.
source_note: Verified Austin 2009, Stat Med 28:3083-3107 (PMID 19757444) via Europe PMC. It defines standardized differences as a covariate balance diagnostic for propensity-matched samples and says nothing about predicting how far an estimate moves. SURFACING_POLICY §2.3 item 2 and §2.4 exist and call this a design-space movement whose thresholds 'are conventions, to be set on the reference journeys', which is a decision rather than a methods reason. materiality_calibration.json's rows_smd entry: 9 cases, all from the dietary-proof journey's simplified pipeline. Its confusion matrix is predicted band 1 -> realized 0/4/4 at bands 0/1/2, one case predicted 0, none predicted 2. The pairs are non-monotone: 0.0037->0.20, 0.0082->0.41, 0.0186->0.63, 0.0229->0.64, 0.1486->0.55, 0.1853->0.12.
note: The tests check the arithmetic against a hand-coded SMD and the open upgrade after the lock (rows x SMD 0.019, realized 0.63 half-widths, band 2). That documents that the proxy under-predicts. No test would fail if rows x SMD had no relation to the realized movement. The thresholds were fitted in-sample to the same 9 cases. The proxy ignores how the leavers differ in exposure and outcome and their leverage, which is what moves a coefficient. Present it as a screening convention ('could bias' unless the screen removes almost nothing), not as a predictor of movement.

source_note: Verified STROBE-nut (Lachat et al. 2016, PLoS Med 13:e1002036) on the publisher page. nut-14: 'Specify if food consumption of total population or consumers only were used to obtain results'. nut-11 covers the handling of non-consumers. As a reporting guideline it asks that the population be stated, which supports treating consumers-only as a different target population, though it gives no estimand theory. That restricting to exposure > 0 targets the effect among consumers is true by definition of the estimand. MODELING_SEQUENCE §1 row 2 and §2 record the ruling ('an estimand change, STROBE-nut nut-14'). The refusal under prediction and the declared-exposure-only rule are design rulings with a stated reason (the model is used on everyone), not literature.
note: The code matches the statement. exposure_form.py:2138 refuses under prediction (domain_for_inference) and refuses for a column other than the declared exposure (domain_of_the_exposure). The option is offered only under inference and only for an exposure with a mass at zero (:1101). The record sentence (:2069) names it an estimand change citing nut-14. The tests check refusals and caption text only. A behavior test is all this needs, since the claim is definitional plus a design rule.

source_note: Verified Janes & Pepe, Biometrics 2008;64(1):1-9 (PMID 17501939), abstract via Europe PMC: 'Matching in studies of classification accuracy: implications for analysis, efficiency, and assessment of incremental value'. It finds that unadjusted accuracy summaries are biased under matching and that matching complicates incremental value. It does not discuss absolute risk, the conditional likelihood or recalibration. The intercept-elimination argument is standard conditional-likelihood theory (e.g. Breslow & Day 1980), but the repo does not cite it. The claim that absolute risk is impossible as a limit of the design is broader than any cited source: absolute risks have been built from matched case-control relative risks combined with external incidence and attributable risk (e.g. Gail et al. 1989). Not from these data alone, then, but not impossible.
note: The code matches the claim (case_control.py:200 eligibility; module docstring 48-53). The tests check only that the refusal fires. The two reasons are sound for one offset applied to these data, but the cited source is about classification accuracy, not risk. 'A limit of the design, not a missing feature' overstates: external incidence plus a risk-factor distribution would allow absolute risk. Reword to 'these data alone cannot give risks; an external incidence and attributable-risk model would be needed', and cite conditional-likelihood theory rather than Janes & Pepe for the intercept argument.

source_note: Verified VanderWeele & Ding, Ann Intern Med 2017;167:268-274 (PMID 28693043) via Europe PMC: the E-value is 'the minimum strength of association, on the risk ratio scale' needed to explain away an association 'conditional on the measured covariates'. That supports bounding a risk ratio and needing risks to get one from a risk difference. Applying it to a standardized (marginal) risk ratio rests on Ding & VanderWeele's bounding results for standardized measures, which are not cited here, so that part is a small step beyond the cited paper.
note: The code matches the claim. stages/effects.py:1484-1486 routes to _marginal_sensitivity when the marginal contrast has an rr; the limits are percentile-bootstrap rr_low/rr_high (models/effects.py:523), and rr_high is +inf when the low risk is 0. The R-backed test (EValue::evalues.RR and evalues.OR) asserts that under a declared risk difference the E-value's measure is 'RR', unconverted, equal to R's to 1e-8, with a reading beginning 'E-value for the marginal risk ratio'. It would fail if the conditional odds ratio were used. It needs R (@needs_r). test_5_the_function_the_causal_lane_calls... checks that a bare risk difference raises.

source_note: No source is cited at case_control.py:839-845 or in the module docstring for this concern. The point is standard matched-design theory: conditioning on the set removes only what members share, so within-set variation in a loosely matched factor can leave residual confounding, and the usual remedy is to add the factor as a covariate in the conditional model (e.g. Breslow & Day 1980; Rothman, Greenland & Lash). Nothing in the repo states that, and nothing supports the size qualifier 'a little'.
test_judged: none found (grep for 'matching within a range' and _not_matched_within finds no test)
note: The trigger is _not_matched_within (case_control.py:917): any matching column with more than one distinct value inside any set, including a single set. 'May confound a little' is an unsupported magnitude, since a wide range can leave material residual confounding. The concern offers no exit, though adjusting for the range-matched factor inside the conditional model is the standard remedy. Suggested wording: 'what the matching left within sets is not removed by the analysis; adding <factor> as a covariate adjusts for it'.

corrected_statement: For a time-to-event outcome under prediction with no declared prediction horizon, the app scores and calibrates predicted risk at the median of the training rows' observed follow-up times (event or censoring, np.median of y['time'], stages/modeling.py:1001-1018), and says so. This is a stated default; the app does not claim it is the appropriate horizon.
source_note: The basis is the internal METHODS_REFERENCE contract (models/validation.py:990-1010: 'Stated: the prediction horizon is declared with the follow-up, else the median follow-up time'), which records a decision with no methods reason. The contract's sources are Graf 1999, McLernon 2023 and Van Calster 2019. I verified McLernon et al., Ann Intern Med 2023;176:105-114 (PMID 36571841) via Europe PMC: predictions are evaluated 'for the event occurring by the end of a fixed time horizon of interest', meaning one chosen for the clinical question. Nothing found endorses the median follow-up as a default.
test_judged: turbotab/core/tests/acceptance/test_ms6_prediction_validation.py::test_1_the_brier_score_at_the_horizon_matches_graf_and_r_survival (checks the computation at a given horizon against R, not the choice of the median)
note: The 'median follow-up time' here is the median of observed times, events included. That is not the reverse Kaplan-Meier median follow-up that epidemiology usually means (Schemper & Smith 1996), and it is shorter whenever events are common, so the wording slightly misnames it. Present it as a convention for when no horizon is given, and ask for a clinically meaningful horizon. The notes say no UI control sets prediction_horizon; I found it only in generated API types, mocks and record composition, which I did not dig into.

source_note: Verified Kalinowski & Humphreys, Addiction 2016;111:1293-1298 (PMID 27073140) via Europe PMC: 'the modal standard drink size was 10 g pure ethanol, but variation was wide (8-20 g)', matching DRINK_GRAMS. The 9% floor is derived in the code comment at readings.py:924-928: with every other source exact, 1/(1 - s) <= 1.10 for s <= 1 - 1/1.10. That arithmetic is correct under its stated assumption. The 0.90-1.10 pass band is the nutrition pack's (turbotab.nutrition PASS_LOW/PASS_HIGH), a convention. BLUEPRINT §14.3's sixth gate is an internal ruling that records the failures (US drinks reconstructing at 1.02 read as grams; InBody protein in kg) and gives the reason for leaving alcohol's unit to the user. 'Alcohol is a minor source' is a judgment.
note: The code matches the statement (readings.py:945-1000; kcal_per_unit at :2312 waits for a recorded unit otherwise). The test builds known-unit fixtures by hand: protein in kg, kcal and kJ, percent of energy, US standard drinks (gate6_fixtures, rng 66001) and a 3%-of-energy protein (rng 66010). It asserts none settles as grams. test_c3 checks that a true gram column does settle. The 9% floor itself is barely tested: with a ratio near 1, the kcal alternative already rejects any protein or carbohydrate source under about 12% (fat about 10%), so the minor-protein fixture would still go unsettled if MINOR_SHARE were removed. The floor is redundant protection, not a load-bearing tested line.

source_note: BLUEPRINT §14 is cited only for the rule that a name leads a guess the user confirms (followed()'s docstring, covariate_guesses.py:341-357). No methods source is given for inferring measurement timing from the outcome's name, and the inventory says so. The downstream with-and-without pair cites PACK08, Schisterman and MODELING_SEQUENCE §1 step 3, but those justify the pair, not the timing inference.
note: The code matches the claim: tokens _INCIDENT (binary only), _FOLLOW_UP, 'follow'+'up', and the _SINCE regex; time_to_event is always followed; v1, t0 and w2 read as nothing. The tests pin name-to-guess behavior and cannot check timing. The reason text states the timing as a fact ('measured at baseline with what you study') and flips pre-filled adjustment answers (outcome_measure left out vs. the declared pair). It should read as an inference from the name, e.g. 'the outcome's name suggests follow-up, so these were probably measured at baseline'. Token edge cases: 'new' or 'final' inside a binary name (new_user, final_diagnosis) would read as follow-up; a time-to-event task does not guarantee baseline covariates when they vary over time.

source_note: Verified Tomova, Arnold, Gilthorpe & Tennant, Am J Clin Nutr 2022;115:189-198 (PMID 34313676) via Europe PMC: 'The standard model and the mathematically identical residual model estimate the average relative causal effect (i.e., a substitution effect) but provide biased estimates even in the absence of confounding'. NUTRITION_PACK §04 (docs/turbotab-next/reference/research/NUTRITION_PACK.md:411-480) records this as SETTLED, gives the several-sources rule ('a substitution for the energy sources not in the model'), and names composite variable bias as the source of that bias. That gives a methods reason, not just a decision.
note: The test is a known-truth simulation for both the standard and residual methods. With all four sources in the model, the 100 kcal protein-for-carbohydrate contrast lies within 2.5 SE of the data-generating 0.600. With two sources it is more than 8 SE away (0.940), and that gap is the composite bias of the omitted sources. It certifies the substitution reading in a linear additive model and the 'only the sources left out' part. It does not check the single-nutrient statement against a truth: that is sourced from Tomova, who also notes the estimate is biased even without confounding, and the app's 'every swap is partly in its place' wording covers this. Under splines or non-identity links the reading is conditional on the other intakes, which the teaching text does not say.

corrected_statement: The engine measures every held-out R², including rows opened from a sealed period, against the training (development) rows' mean: models/metrics.py, 'R² is measured against the training rows' mean ... on the held-out rows', citing Staerk et al. 2024 and audit MA-09. That R² therefore compares the model with the deployable no-predictor model. BEATS_PREDICT §17 ruling 7, 'against the cycle's own mean (0.18)', is a doc ruling the code does not implement and that the engine's own rationale contradicts.
source_note: The only basis is the orchestrator ruling of 2026-10-11 (BEATS_PREDICT.md:1494), a decision with a one-word reason ('conventional and conservative'). 'Conservative' is true by algebra, since the period's own mean minimizes the total sum of squares, so own-mean R² <= development-mean R² always, with equality when the means coincide. 'Conventional' matches scikit-learn's r2_score. The engine's own documentation (metrics.py:13-19) argues the opposite, quoting Staerk et al. 2024 that the training-mean definition 'may generally be preferable based on theoretical reasons'. BEATS_PREDICT's R5 Table 2 (line 988-989) also reports 'R² 0.20 ... against the development mean'. I did not fetch Staerk et al.
test_judged: turbotab/core/tests/test_modeling.py (holdout test at lines 200-225: asserts holdout r2 equals R² against the training mean and is NOT scikit-learn's own-mean r2_score)
note: The doc ruling contradicts the engine and the same document's Table 2. The existing test would fail if the ruling were implemented. Someone must decide which definition the opened cycle reports. If both appear (0.18 own-mean vs 0.20 development-mean), each must be labeled with its reference mean. The ruling's other half, judging deployability by RMSE against the development mean's RMSE, agrees with the engine's baseline comparison.

corrected_statement: On a total-energy column, an intake screen that would remove more than half the rows (MOST_ROWS = 0.5) is refused even after the unit has been recorded (decisions._screens_keep_most_rows, code screen_removes_most_rows). The exits re-read the bounds in another unit (kJ, a multi-day or weekly total) wherever that keeps at least half, or drop the rule. The finding words treat the unit as the likelier error than the people, with a child's kJ, an athlete's intake and a weekly total as examples. Separately, an energy screen waits for the unit to be recorded (energy_unit_unconfirmed).
source_note: Audit IN-07 (docs/turbotab-next/audit/AUDIT_REPORT.md:446-451) exists and recommends 'refuse a screen that would remove more than half the rows, with a units exit'. Its methods reason is an observed failure: a kJ column read as kcal lost 764-989 of 800-1,000 rows. That shows unit errors produce mass exclusions, but no source gives the 50% threshold or the claim that the unit is the likelier error. Those are conventions.
test_judged: turbotab/core/tests/acceptance/test_wp13_recognizers.py (the children_kj case asserting refusal code screen_removes_most_rows with kcal recorded, line ~1184)
note: The test checks refusal behavior and exits on a kJ fixture. Nothing tests the 'likelier error' claim, and nothing could from these data. 'Until the unit is stated' is inaccurate: the test shows the refusal still fires after the unit is recorded as kcal. A legitimately low- or high-intake sample (an inpatient ward, an athletes' cohort) can never apply its screen as written. Present the 50% as a convention ('a screen that removes most rows usually means a unit mismatch'), and consider an explicit override.

corrected_statement: The Predict design (BEATS_PREDICT M1 and §9 ruling 13) says the model should read only predictors recorded at its intended moment of use, for example no 24-hour recall for a clinic use, because a predictor known only after that moment is not available in use (PROBAST 2.3). The engine does not implement this yet. WALKABLE_PLAN.md:48 and :143 record the moment of use as 'missing in the engine too: no q:moment_of_use' (P3, unbuilt), and no code reads a moment of use to choose predictors.
source_note: PROBAST (Wolff et al. 2019, Ann Intern Med 170:51) signalling question 2.3, 'Are all predictors available at the time the model is intended to be used?'. I confirmed the wording and number 2.3 through a PMC systematic review that tabulates it (PMC12703889, via Europe PMC full text); the probast.org PDF fetched but could not be text-extracted here. 2.3 asks about availability as a risk-of-bias question. The app's paraphrase, that such a model 'looks better in a paper than in use', fits PROBAST's rationale but I did not verify that wording in the source. Ruling 13 is an internal design ruling that cites PROBAST 2.3 as its methods reason.
test_judged: none (no q:moment_of_use or predictor-by-moment code exists to test)
note: Sound and sourced as a design principle, but the 'user sees' Why? text exists only in a beats document. Before the card ships, the engine needs P3 (moment of use compiled to predictor roles) and a test that a predictor recorded after the moment is excluded. Until then the app must not claim that only moment-available predictors are read.
